deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The previous page states a theorem and begins its proof. The theorem: for every convergent (resp. divergent) series sum a_n one can find a convergent (resp. divergent) series sum b_n that converges (resp. diverges) more slowly. For the convergent case this means lim b_n/a_n = infinity. The proof begun there uses regrouping by repetition, a_1 + a_2/2 + a_2/2 + a_3/3 + a_3/3 + a_3/3 + ..., which is the 'umgekehrt zusammenfassen' (reverse grouping) mentioned here.

(1) Convergence criteria. 'Convergenzbedingungen: a_n/a_{n+1} > 1, n(a_n/a_{n+1} - 1) < 1 etc. nach derselben Methode beweisen. Oder durch umgekehrt zusammenfassen.'
- Two tests in the scale of ratio tests are named. The first is d'Alembert's ratio test, in the form a_n/a_{n+1} > 1. The second is Raabe's test, written here with the divergence inequality n(a_n/a_{n+1} - 1) < 1. Raabe gives convergence if n(a_n/a_{n+1} - 1) >= r > 1 for large n, and divergence if it is <= 1 for large n. 'etc.' points to the rest of the scale (Bertrand/De Morgan, with log terms).
- My reading: by the same method (constructing a slower series) one shows that each criterion of this hierarchy is non-exhaustive. There are always series beyond its reach, so no last criterion exists (du Bois-Reymond, Pringsheim). Alternatively the same is shown by the reverse grouping.

(2) The limiting series. 'Die Grenzreihe von a_n/a_{n+1} = 1 + 1/n + 1/n^2 + ... = [n/(n-1)] ist, divergirt.'
- Summing the geometric series gives 1 + 1/n + 1/n^2 + ... = 1/(1 - 1/n) = n/(n-1). The page shows the right-hand side as 1/(n-1), which is a slip or abbreviation; the value must be n/(n-1).
- From a_n/a_{n+1} = n/(n-1) we get a_{n+1} = a_n (n-1)/n. Hence a_n = C/(n-1), the harmonic series, which diverges.
- The point (filled in by me): here a_n/a_{n+1} > 1 for every n. Moreover n(a_n/a_{n+1} - 1) = n/(n-1) > 1 for every n. Yet the series diverges.
- So the ratio test needs ratio >= q > 1, and Raabe's test needs a bound r > 1 uniformly, not merely a pointwise strict inequality. The 'Grenzreihe' sits exactly on the boundary of Raabe's criterion, since n(a_n/a_{n+1} - 1) tends to 1.

(3) Example (written as 'Beispiel' and then heavily struck through). The series is 1 + 1/2^{1+1/2} + 1/3^{1+1/3} + ..., i.e. a_n = n^{-(1+1/n)}.
- Hilbert begins n(a_n/a_{n+1} - 1) = n( n^{1+1/n} / (n+1)^{1+1/(n+1)} - 1 ). This quotient is inverted: in fact a_n/a_{n+1} = (n+1)^{1+1/(n+1)} / n^{1+1/n}. That may be why the computation was abandoned.
- Correct continuation (mine): a_n/a_{n+1} = (1 + 1/n) * exp( ln(n+1)/(n+1) - ln n/n ) = 1 + 1/n + (1 - ln n)/n^2 + O(ln n/n^3).
- Hence n(a_n/a_{n+1} - 1) = 1 + (1 - ln n)/n + ..., which tends to 1 from below for n >= 3.
- Raabe's divergence criterion therefore applies. This agrees with a_n ~ 1/n, since n^{1/n} -> 1. The example is a series whose general term is 'almost' n^{-1-epsilon' but which diverges, and for which the plain ratio test fails.

(4) Reference. 'vergl. Weierstrass Functionenlehre: Theorie der analytischen Facultaeten.' This points to Weierstrass, 'Ueber die Theorie der analytischen Facultaeten', J. reine angew. Math. 51 (1856). There the criterion for series with a_{n+1}/a_n = 1 - mu/n + O(n^{-1-epsilon}) is treated (Gauss/Weierstrass test).

(5) Proof of the 'obigen Saetze' (the slower-convergence theorem of the previous page), convergent case.
- Let R_N = sum_{n>N} a_n with a_n >= 0.
- Choose N_1 with R_{N_1} < 1/2, and multiply all terms beyond N_1 by 2.
- Then choose N_2 > N_1 with R_{N_2} < 1/4, and double again, and so on.
- The new series is b_n = 2^k a_n for N_k < n <= N_{k+1}. Then b_n/a_n = 2^k -> infinity.
- Convergence needs sum_k 2^k (R_{N_k} - R_{N_{k+1}}) < infinity.
- With thresholds exactly 2^{-k}, the block bound is only 2^k R_{N_k} < 1, which is not summable. One must choose the N_k farther out, e.g. R_{N_k} < 4^{-k}; then the blocks are bounded by 2^{-k} and the sum converges.
- The divergent case is analogous ('umgekehrt'): go until the partial sum exceeds 1, 2, 4, ... and halve the factors, giving b_n/a_n -> 0.
errors: The geometric sum 1 + 1/n + 1/n^2 + ... equals n/(n-1), not 1/(n-1) as written (slip or shorthand). With n/(n-1) the recurrence gives a_n ~ 1/(n-1), the divergent harmonic series, which is what the text asserts.

In the struck-out example the quotient is inverted. For a_n = n^{-(1+1/n)} one has a_n/a_{n+1} = (n+1)^{1+1/(n+1)}/n^{1+1/n}, not n^{1+1/n}/(n+1)^{1+1/(n+1)}. With the written expression n(...-1) tends to -1 instead of 1. The correct value tends to 1 from below like 1 + (1 - ln n)/n.

The proof sketch as stated (remainder < 2^{-k}, factor doubled each time, so factor 2^k) does not by itself guarantee convergence. Block k contributes 2^k(R_{N_k} - R_{N_{k+1}}), bounded only by 2^k R_{N_k} < 1, which is not summable. A counterexample is R_{N_k} ~ c 2^{-k}, giving blocks ~ c/2. The fix is to take thresholds decreasing faster than the factors grow, e.g. R_{N_k} < 4^{-k} with factor 2^k. Since N_k may be taken arbitrarily far out, the idea is sound but the stated constants are insufficient.

The criteria in the first line are given only schematically: 'a_n/a_{n+1} > 1' without a uniform bound q > 1, and Raabe with '< 1' (the divergence direction). This is acceptable as a note, and the Grenzreihe remark itself shows why the pointwise inequality is insufficient.

results.what: For every convergent (divergent) positive series there is one converging (diverging) more slowly, b_n/a_n -> infinity (resp. 0), proved by blockwise doubling of the tail terms (or halving after partial-sum thresholds).
results.modern_name: Abel-Dini / du Bois-Reymond theorem on non-existence of a slowest convergent/divergent series (no universal comparison test)
results.usually_credited_to: N. H. Abel (divergent case, 1828 posthumous note), U. Dini (1867), P. du Bois-Reymond (1873); later systematized by Hadamard (1894) and Pringsheim (1890)

results.what: The ratio test and Raabe's test (and the whole logarithmic scale) are not exhaustive and require uniform bounds; the boundary series a_n/a_{n+1} = n/(n-1) is the harmonic series, which diverges although n(a_n/a_{n+1}-1) > 1 for all n.
results.modern_name: Raabe's test (Raabe 1832), d'Alembert ratio test, boundary case of the Kummer/Bertrand hierarchy
results.usually_credited_to: d'Alembert, J. L. Raabe (1832), Bertrand (1842), Kummer (1835); non-exhaustiveness: du Bois-Reymond, Pringsheim

results.what: Example: sum n^{-(1+1/n)} diverges; Raabe quantity n(a_n/a_{n+1}-1) = 1 + (1 - ln n)/n + ... < 1.
results.modern_name: Standard textbook example of a divergent series with exponent tending to 1 from above

results.what: Reference to Weierstrass's 1856 Crelle paper on analytic factorials (convergence criterion for a_{n+1}/a_n = 1 - mu/n + O(n^{-1-epsilon})).

deep.surprise_reason: These are early study notes on standard 19th-century series theory: the Abel-Dini-du Bois-Reymond theorem, Raabe/ratio criteria, the harmonic series as a boundary case, and a pointer to Weierstrass 1856. The neighbouring page explicitly credits a related idea to Hurwitz. Nothing goes beyond the textbook literature of the 1870s-80s; the only interest is biographical (Hilbert's early reading, Hurwitz's influence).

checkable.asserts: a_n = 1/(n-1) satisfies a_n/a_{n+1} = n/(n-1), so the boundary series is harmonic (divergent)
For the boundary series the Raabe quantity equals n/(n-1) > 1 for all n, yet the series diverges
Correct Raabe quantity for a_n = n^{-(1+1/n)} tends to 1
Hilbert's (inverted) expression tends to -1, confirming the inversion slip
n(a_n/a_{n+1}-1) = 1 - (ln n)/n + o(ln n/n), hence < 1 eventually, so Raabe gives divergence
n^{-(1+1/n)} ~ 1/n, so sum n^{-(1+1/n)} diverges by limit comparison with the harmonic series
With thresholds R_{N_k} < 4^{-k} and factors 2^k the modified series converges (block sum bounded by sum 2^{-k}), repairing the proof
With remainders ~ 2^{-k} and factors 2^k the block contributions ~ 1/2 need not be summable (gap in stated constants)

transcription_corrections: Right-hand side '= 1/(n-1)': the image appears to show '1/(n-1)', but the intended value is n/(n-1) = 1/(1-1/n); the transcription is faithful to a slip in the manuscript.

'Beispiel' and the two formulas below it (the series 1 + 1/2^{1+1/2} + 1/3^{1+1/3} + ... and the Raabe quotient) are crossed by long diagonal strokes; the transcription correctly marks them as deleted.
In the struck-out formula the image shows n^{1+1/n} in the numerator and (n+1)^{1+1/(n+1)} in the denominator, followed by a closing brace before '-1', i.e. n( n^{1+1/n}/(n+1)^{1+1/(n+1)} - 1 ).
'multiplici- wieder mit 2 etc.' should read 'multiplicire wieder mit 2 etc.'.
Title reads 'Convergenzbedingungen' (with 'etc.' after the Raabe inequality); the deleted fragment before 'nach' is likely 'Zu' or 'So', not certain.
